```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| message: false

# Carried over from week 9: the data, the plot theme, the fits and the party
# colors that the slides from "Example: controlling for party" onward use
library(tidyverse)
options(width = 110)    # the code font is small, so let printed output run wider

# 2024 ANES: the Trump thermometer and the four-item hostile sexism scale
# (data/prepare_data.R builds the extract from the full release)
anes <- read_csv("data/anes24_sexism.csv") |>
  filter(!is.na(ft_trump), !is.na(hostile_sexism)) |>
  mutate(party = case_when(pid7 <= 3 ~ "Democrat", pid7 == 4 ~ "Independent",
                           pid7 >= 5 ~ "Republican"))

theme_reg <- theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(colour = "#333333"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F7F7F7", colour = NA))

fit_hs <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism, data = anes)
fit_rr <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + racial_resentment, data = anes)
b_hs <- coef(fit_hs)
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)

# Each party's respondents in its color. Respondents in all three parties
# share the 17 values of X, so each party's points are nudged sideways a
# little to keep them from hiding one another
party_cols <- c(Democrat = "#0479a8", Independent = "#b8860b", Republican = "#c5050c")
party_pts <- anes |>
  filter(!is.na(party)) |>
  mutate(x = hostile_sexism + c(Democrat = -0.014, Independent = 0, Republican = 0.014)[party])
```

## Ordinary Least Squares

```{r}
#| label: ols-setup
#| include: false

# A small fake sample for the least squares animation (ols-anim/ols.js): a
# horizontal line at c0, its residuals and their squares, the line moving to
# the OLS fit, then the OLS residuals lifted out and chained to show they sum
# to zero. The script takes the stage it opens on and the stage its last
# fragment reaches
set.seed(1)
ols_x <- sort(round(runif(12, 1, 9), 2))
ols_y <- round(2 + 0.6 * ols_x + rnorm(12, 0, 1.2), 2)
ols_b <- coef(lm(ols_y ~ ols_x))
ols_data <- jsonlite::toJSON(list(x = ols_x, y = ols_y, c0 = 7.5,
                                  b0 = unname(ols_b[1]), b1 = unname(ols_b[2]),
                                  xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10)),
                             auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA)
ols_anim <- function(from, to) {
  cat("```{=html}",
      '<div class="ol-anim"></div>',
      "<script>",
      "(", readLines("ols-anim/ols.js"), ")(document.currentScript.previousElementSibling,",
      ols_data, ", { from: ", from, ", to: ", to, " });",
      "</script>",
      rep('<span class="fragment ol-step"></span>', to - from),
      "```", sep = "\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ols_anim(0, 7)
```

## OLS for estimating the CEF

::: {.incremental}

- We'll show that under i.i.d. sampling, OLS is consistent for the **Best Linear Predictor**
  - The linear combination of $X_i$ that *minimizes* the mean squared prediction error.
- But we want to estimate the **CEF** $\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i]$
  - When is OLS consistent for the **conditional expectation function**?
- When the **CEF** is the **BLP**!

  $$\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i] = \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}$$

- When is the CEF linear?
  - **Saturated** models: every covariate is discrete and there is a dummy for every combination of values (e.g. the three party categories)
  - Otherwise, linearity is an **assumption** about the functional form
  - Remember, this is *linearity in parameters* given a particular $\mathbf{X}$
    - Adding more terms to $\mathbf{X}$ may make linearity more plausible!


:::

## Interpreting multiple regression coefficients

::: {.incremental}

- With a **bivariate** regression, interpreting the coefficient on $X_i$ is straightforward
  
  $$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\widehat{\Cov}(X_i, Y_i)}{\widehat{\Var}(X_i)}$$
  
- The difference in the expectation of $Y_i$ between respondents whose $X_i$ differs by **one unit**

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x + 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] &= \big(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (x + 1)\big) - \big(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\big) \\
  &= \beta_1
  \end{aligned}
  $$

:::

## Interpreting multiple regression coefficients

::: {.incremental}

- However, with a **multivariate** regression, the coefficient captures a different relationship.

- The difference in the expected $Y_i$ between respondents whose $X_{i1}$ differs by one unit...
  - ...**holding the other covariates fixed**.

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  &\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_{i1} = x_1 + 1, X_{i2} = x_2, \dotsc, X_{i,k-1} = x_{k-1}] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_{i1} = x_1, X_{i2} = x_2, \dotsc, X_{i,k-1} = x_{k-1}] \\
  &\qquad = \big(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_1 + 1) + \beta_2 x_2 + \dotsc + \beta_{k-1} x_{k-1}\big) - \big(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dotsc + \beta_{k-1} x_{k-1}\big) \\
  &\qquad = \beta_1
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  - We'll often talk about interpreting $\beta_1$ in terms of the relationships between $X$ and $Y$ after **controlling for** or **conditioning on** the other covariates

- What is OLS **actually doing**? 
  - We're not physically controlling anything!
  - The **Frisch-Waugh-Lovell** theorem gives us a way of thinking about multivariate regression coefficients in terms of a **residuals**-on-**residuals** regression.

:::

## Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem

::: {.incremental}

- Split the regressors into the one we care about, $X_{i1}$, and **everything else**, $\mathbf{X}_{i,-1}$ (which includes the intercept)

  $$Y_i = \hat{\beta}_1 X_{i1} + \mathbf{X}_{i,-1}^\prime\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-1} + \hat{e}_i$$

- **Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (FWL)**: we can get the same $\hat{\beta}_1$ from three regressions
  1. Regress $Y_i$ on $\mathbf{X}_{i,-1}$ and keep the residuals, $\tilde{Y}_i$
  2. Regress $X_{i1}$ on $\mathbf{X}_{i,-1}$ and keep the residuals, $\tilde{X}_{i1}$
  3. Regress $\tilde{Y}_i$ on $\tilde{X}_{i1}$. 

- The slope is **exactly** $\hat{\beta}_1$

  $$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\widehat{\Cov}(\tilde{X}_{i1}, \tilde{Y}_i)}{\widehat{\Var}(\tilde{X}_{i1})}$$


:::


## What FWL tells us

::: {.incremental}

- $\hat{\beta}_1$ only uses the variation in $X_{i1}$ that is **not linearly predicted** by the other covariates to explain $Y_i$

- "Controlling for" $\mathbf{X}_{i,-1}$ means **partialling out** its linear relationship with both $X_{i1}$ and $Y_i$
  - If $X_{i1}$ is **uncorrelated** with the other covariates in the sample, then adding those covariates doesn't change $\hat{\beta}_1$

- Remember that the "partialling out" is **linear**
  - If $\mathbf{X}_{i,-1}$ is related to $X_{i1}$ or $Y_i$ in a way that the linear regression does not capture, that relationship is still in the residuals and might be attributed to $X_{i1}$.

:::

## Visualizing FWL

```{r}
#| label: fwl-setup
#| include: false

# A Simpson's paradox for the FWL animation (fwl-anim/fwl.js), after
# ryxcommar's "Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, animated": three groups of X2 whose
# means of X1 and Y rise together, while Y falls with X1 within each group.
# Partialling X2 out of Y and then out of X1 turns the pooled slope (about
# +0.6) into the within-group slope of Y ~ X1 + X2 (about -0.7)
set.seed(2)
fwl_g <- rep(1:3, each = 15)
fwl_m <- c(2.5, 5, 7.5)[fwl_g]
fwl_x <- round(fwl_m + rnorm(45, 0, 1.1), 2)
fwl_y <- round(fwl_m - 0.8 * (fwl_x - fwl_m) + rnorm(45, 0, 0.5), 2)
fwl_b1 <- unname(coef(lm(fwl_y ~ fwl_x + factor(fwl_g)))[2])
fwl_data <- jsonlite::toJSON(list(x = fwl_x, y = fwl_y, g = fwl_g, b1 = fwl_b1,
                                  xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10)),
                             auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA)
fwl_anim <- function(from, to) {
  cat("```{=html}",
      '<div class="fw-anim"></div>',
      "<script>",
      "(", readLines("fwl-anim/fwl.js"), ")(document.currentScript.previousElementSibling,",
      fwl_data, ", { from: ", from, ", to: ", to, " });",
      "</script>",
      rep('<span class="fragment fw-step"></span>', to - from),
      "```", sep = "\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fwl_anim(0, 7)
```

## Example: controlling for party

::: {.incremental}

- In our example, $\mathbf{X}_{i,-1}$ is the intercept plus the Independent and Republican dummies
  - A regression on a **full set** of indicators predicts each category's **mean**

- So partialling out party just subtracts each respondent's **party mean**

  $$\tilde{X}_{i1} = X_{i1} - \bar{X}_{\text{party}(i)} \qquad \tilde{Y}_i = Y_i - \bar{Y}_{\text{party}(i)}$$

- $\hat{\beta}_1$ is the slope using only the **within-party** variation
  - Differences in hostile sexism **between** the parties contribute nothing to $\hat{\beta}_1$

:::

## FWL in R

```{r}
anes_p <- anes |> filter(!is.na(party))   # the same respondents in every regression

# The full regression
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + party, data = anes_p)), 2)

# Steps 1 and 2: partial party out of the outcome and out of hostile sexism
anes_p$y_tilde <- resid(lm(ft_trump ~ party, data = anes_p))
anes_p$x_tilde <- resid(lm(hostile_sexism ~ party, data = anes_p))

# Step 3: residuals on residuals
round(coef(lm(y_tilde ~ x_tilde, data = anes_p)), 2)
```


## Interacting with partisanship

::: {.incremental}

- To let the **slope** on hostile sexism differ between parties too we add **interactions**
  - The products of $X_i$ with each dummy

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i + \hat{\beta}_2 X_i^{\text{Ind}} + \hat{\beta}_3 X_i^{\text{Rep}} + \hat{\beta}_4 X_i X_i^{\text{Ind}} + \hat{\beta}_5 X_i X_i^{\text{Rep}}$$

- Within each party, the fit is still a line in $X_i$, but now each has its own intercept **and** slope

  $$\begin{aligned} \text{Democrats:} \quad & \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \\ \text{Independents:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2) + (\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_4) X_i \\ \text{Republicans:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_3) + (\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_5) X_i \end{aligned}$$

- $\hat{\beta}_1$ is now the slope among **Democrats** (the baseline), and $\hat{\beta}_4$, $\hat{\beta}_5$ are **differences in slopes** relative to Democrats
- With every interaction in, this is the **same** as fitting a separate OLS line within each party

:::

## Interacting with partisanship

```{r}
#| label: fit-party-int
#| include: false
fit_pint <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * party, data = anes)
b_pi <- coef(fit_pint)
# Each party's slope: the baseline slope plus its difference
slope_p <- b_pi["hostile_sexism"] +
  c(0, b_pi["hostile_sexism:partyIndependent"], b_pi["hostile_sexism:partyRepublican"])
```

```{r}
# x * z in a formula adds x, z, and their product x:z
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * party, data = anes)), 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-align: center

# The party lines again, now each with its own slope
party_int_lines <- tibble(party = names(party_cols),
                          a = b_pi[1] + c(0, b_pi["partyIndependent"], b_pi["partyRepublican"]),
                          b = slope_p)
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = party_pts, aes(x, ft_trump, colour = party), alpha = 0.06, size = 3,
             stroke = 0) +
  geom_segment(data = party_int_lines, aes(x = 0, xend = 1, y = a, yend = a + b, colour = party),
               linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_text(data = party_int_lines,
            aes(1.03, a + b, label = sprintf("%s (slope %.1f)", party, b), colour = party),
            hjust = 0, size = 5.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = party_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.35), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Hostile sexism", y = "Trump thermometer") +
  theme_reg
```

- Slopes actually aren't that different!

## Interacting with education

::: {.incremental}

- Does the slope on hostile sexism differ by **education**? 
  - Let $X_i^{\text{Col}} = I(\text{college degree}_i)$ and add its product with $X_i$

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i + \hat{\beta}_2 X_i^{\text{Col}} + \hat{\beta}_3 X_i X_i^{\text{Col}}$$

- Within each education group, the fit is a line in $X_i$ with its own intercept **and** slope

  $$\begin{aligned} \text{No college degree:} \quad & \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \\ \text{College degree:} \quad & (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_2) + (\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3) X_i \end{aligned}$$

- $\hat{\beta}_1$ is the slope among respondents **without** a degree (the baseline), and $\hat{\beta}_3$ is the **difference in slopes** for college graduates

:::

## A second continuous covariate

::: {.incremental}

- **Racial resentment**: a three question measure from @kinder1996divided, also averaged and re-scaled to $[0, 1]$
  - Correlated with hostile sexism: $r = `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(anes$hostile_sexism, anes$racial_resentment, use = "complete.obs"))`$

- With two continuous covariates, the fit is a **plane** over $(X_{i1}, X_{i2})$

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_{i1} + \hat{\beta}_2 X_{i2}$$

:::

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + racial_resentment, data = anes)), 2)
```

:::

::: {.incremental}

- After partialling **racial resentment** out of both the outcome and hostile sexism, the slope on hostile sexism is `r f1(coef(fit_rr)[2])`, also down from the unconditional `r f1(b_hs[2])`

:::

## In three dimensions {.plane-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: false

# The two-covariate OLS fit as a surface through the 3D scatterplot. The
# animation (plane-anim/plane.js) turns the camera slowly while the slide is
# up; its fragments fade in a surface and bend it from the coefficients
# `from` into `beta` (each b0 + b1 x + b2 y + b3 xy), then draw the lines
# along it where racial resentment is held fixed
rr_pts <- anes |> filter(!is.na(racial_resentment))
b_rr <- coef(fit_rr)

plane_axis <- function(title, ...) {
  list(title = list(text = title, font = list(size = 15)), gridcolor = "#d9d9d9",
       zeroline = FALSE, showspikes = FALSE, showbackground = TRUE,
       backgroundcolor = "#EFEFEF", tickfont = list(size = 12), tickangle = 0, ...)
}

plane_widget <- function(beta, from, titles) {
  beta <- unname(c(beta, 0)[1:4])    # no interaction: b3 = 0
  from <- unname(c(from, 0)[1:4])
  surf <- function(h, r) beta[1] + beta[2] * h + beta[3] * r + beta[4] * h * r
  # A fine grid, since with an interaction the surface is curved
  pg <- seq(0, 1, 0.05)
  plane_z <- outer(pg, pg, \(r, h) surf(h, r))   # rows are y
  slice_rr <- c(0, 0.5, 1)
  slices <- list(x = unlist(lapply(slice_rr, \(r) c(0, 1, NA))),
                 y = unlist(lapply(slice_rr, \(r) c(r, r, NA))),
                 z = unlist(lapply(slice_rr, \(r) c(surf(0, r), surf(1, r), NA))))

  # Trace order matters: plane.js addresses traces by index
  p <- plotly::plot_ly(width = 1000, height = 560) |>
    plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers", x = rr_pts$hostile_sexism,
                      y = rr_pts$racial_resentment, z = rr_pts$ft_trump, opacity = 0.12,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "#333333", line = list(width = 0)),
                      hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    plotly::add_surface(x = pg, y = pg, z = plane_z, opacity = 0.35, showscale = FALSE,
                        colorscale = list(c(0, "#0479a8"), c(1, "#0479a8")),
                        lighting = list(ambient = 1, diffuse = 0, specular = 0, fresnel = 0),
                        hoverinfo = "skip", visible = FALSE) |>
    plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines", x = slices$x, y = slices$y,
                      z = slices$z, line = list(color = "#c5050c", width = 7),
                      connectgaps = FALSE, hoverinfo = "skip", visible = FALSE) |>
    plotly::layout(
      showlegend = FALSE,
      paper_bgcolor = "#F7F7F7",
      margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 0, b = 0),
      font = list(family = "Red Hat Text, sans-serif", color = "#333333"),
      scene = list(
        xaxis = plane_axis("Hostile sexism", range = c(0, 1), tickvals = c(0, 0.5, 1)),
        yaxis = plane_axis("Racial resentment", range = c(0, 1), tickvals = c(0, 0.5, 1)),
        zaxis = plane_axis("Trump thermometer", range = c(-12, 105),
                           tickvals = seq(0, 100, 25)),
        aspectmode = "manual", aspectratio = list(x = 1.6, y = 1.6, z = 1.15),
        camera = list(projection = list(type = "orthographic")),   # set by the animation
        dragmode = "turntable", hovermode = FALSE
      )
    ) |>
    plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE, doubleClick = FALSE)

  p <- htmlwidgets::onRender(
    p,
    paste(readLines("plane-anim/plane.js"), collapse = "\n"),
    data = list(grid = pg, beta = beta, from = from, titles = titles)
  )

  # One empty fragment per animation step after the first
  htmltools::tagList(
    p,
    lapply(seq_len(length(titles) - 1), function(i) htmltools::span(class = "fragment pl-step"))
  )
}

# The plane rises from flat, at the mean of Y
plane_widget(b_rr, from = mean(rr_pts$ft_trump),
             titles = c("", "The regression plane", "Holding racial resentment fixed"))
```

## Interacting two continuous covariates

```{r}
#| label: fit-rr-int
#| include: false

# The hostile sexism x racial resentment interaction and its marginal effect
# of hostile sexism, b1 + b3 z, over the range of racial resentment, with a
# 95% band from HC0 (robust) standard errors
fit_rint <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * racial_resentment, data = rr_pts)
b_ri <- coef(fit_rint)
V_ri <- sandwich::vcovHC(fit_rint, type = "HC0")
me_line <- tibble(z = seq(0, 1, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(est = b_ri[2] + b_ri[4] * z,
         se = sqrt(V_ri[2, 2] + z^2 * V_ri[4, 4] + 2 * z * V_ri[2, 4]),
         lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se)

# The binning estimator of Hainmueller, Mummolo and Xu: terciles of racial
# resentment, each with its own intercept, slope on hostile sexism, slope on
# racial resentment and interaction, with racial resentment centered at the
# bin's median so that each bin's slope on hostile sexism is the marginal
# effect at that median
rr_bin <- rr_pts |>
  mutate(bin = cut(racial_resentment, quantile(racial_resentment, 0:3 / 3),
                   include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("Low", "Middle", "High"))) |>
  mutate(med = median(racial_resentment), zc = racial_resentment - med, .by = bin)
fit_bin <- lm(ft_trump ~ 0 + bin + bin:hostile_sexism + bin:zc + bin:hostile_sexism:zc,
              data = rr_bin)
V_bin <- sandwich::vcovHC(fit_bin, type = "HC0")
alpha_j <- paste0("bin", levels(rr_bin$bin), ":hostile_sexism")
me_bins <- tibble(bin = levels(rr_bin$bin), z = sort(unique(rr_bin$med)),
                  est = coef(fit_bin)[alpha_j], se = sqrt(diag(V_bin)[alpha_j]),
                  lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se,
                  lin = b_ri[2] + b_ri[4] * z)

# How many respondents sit at each of racial resentment's 13 values: drawn as
# a histogram along the bottom of the marginal effects plots, scaled so the
# tallest bar is 18 points high
rr_hist <- count(rr_pts, z = racial_resentment) |> mutate(h = 18 * n / max(n))

# Floor and ceiling of the thermometer in the outer terciles
rr_floor <- with(filter(rr_bin, bin == "Low"), mean(ft_trump == 0))
rr_ceil <- with(filter(rr_bin, bin == "High"), mean(ft_trump == 100))
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)

me_plot <- function(bins = FALSE) {
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_rect(data = rr_hist, aes(xmin = z - 0.03, xmax = z + 0.03, ymin = 0, ymax = h),
              fill = "#d9d9d9") +
    annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 21, label = "Respondents at each level of racial resentment",
             size = 4.5, colour = "#777777") +
    geom_ribbon(data = me_line, aes(z, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#c5050c", alpha = 0.15) +
    geom_line(data = me_line, aes(z, est), colour = "#c5050c", linewidth = 1.6) +
    annotate("text", x = 1.02, y = tail(me_line$est, 1), label = "Linear\ninteraction",
             hjust = 0, size = 5.5, colour = "#c5050c", lineheight = 0.9)
  if (bins) {
    p <- p +
      geom_errorbar(data = me_bins, aes(z, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.025,
                    colour = "#0479a8", linewidth = 1.1) +
      geom_point(data = me_bins, aes(z, est), colour = "#0479a8", fill = "#0479a8",
                 shape = 21, size = 4.5, stroke = 1.5) +
      # Each label on the side of its interval away from the line
      geom_text(data = me_bins,
                aes(z, if_else(est < lin, lo, hi), label = paste(bin, "tercile"),
                    vjust = if_else(est < lin, 1.8, -0.8)),
                size = 5, colour = "#0479a8")
  }
  p +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 80, 20)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.12), ylim = c(0, 88)) +
    labs(x = "Racial resentment",
         y = "Marginal effect of\nhostile sexism") +
    theme_reg
}
```

::: {.incremental}

- A linear interaction with two **continuous** covariates adds the **product** of hostile sexism and racial resentment to the equation.

  $$\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_{i1} + \hat{\beta}_2 X_{i2} + \hat{\beta}_3 X_{i1} X_{i2}$$

- Holding $X_{i2}$ at a value $x_2$, we're still estimating a **line** for $X_{i1}$, but its slope now **depends on** $x_2$

  $$\big[\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (x_1 + 1) + \hat{\beta}_2 x_2 + \hat{\beta}_3 (x_1 + 1) x_2\big] - \big[\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_1 + \hat{\beta}_2 x_2 + \hat{\beta}_3 x_1 x_2\big] = \hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3 x_2$$

  - The **marginal 'effect'** of $X_{i1}$ at $X_{i2} = x_2$. (be careful though, this is just a **slope** - we're not yet making a causal claim).
  - $\hat{\beta}_1$ alone is the slope at $X_{i2} = 0$ - sometimes this is meaningful, sometimes it isn't!

:::

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
round(coef(lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism * racial_resentment, data = anes)), 2)
```

:::

- The slope on hostile sexism rises from `r f1(b_ri[2])` at the lowest racial resentment to `r f1(b_ri[2] + b_ri[4])` at the highest, a **straight line** with slope $\hat{\beta}_3 = `r f1(b_ri[4])`$
  - The band is a 95% confidence interval (using robust HC0 SEs)
- The gray bars show where the **data** are. Always plot the marginal effect against the distribution of the moderator

## Careful with linear interactions!

::: {.incremental}

- $\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3 x_2$ assumes the slope on $X_{i1}$ changes at a **constant rate** in $X_{i2}$
  - Where few respondents have a given $X_{i2}$ (**weak common support**), the predicted marginal effect relies heavily on the functional form assumption!

- @hainmueller2019much recommend a check that just uses **bins** of the effect modifier
  - Estimate separate slopes and intercepts **within each bin**
  - Think of what we did before: comparing the **noisy** binning approach with the **efficient** but potentially **biased** regression

:::

## Binned marginal effects

```{r}

#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
me_plot(bins = TRUE)
```

::: {.incremental}

- The bins differ from the linear interaction results!
  - The slope is **steepest** in the middle tercile (`r f1(me_bins$est[2])`) and **flattest** in the top one (`r f1(me_bins$est[3])`), where the linear interaction puts its largest slope (`r f1(me_bins$lin[3])`)
  - The linear interaction **forced** a monotone pattern onto a hump
- Likely because the thermometer is **bounded**: 
  - Little room to move at either end, so the marginal "effects" get compressed at the tails.

:::

## Consistency of OLS

::: {.incremental}

- We've made a few regularity assumptions to ensure the **BLP** exists

- What do we need to make OLS **consistent** for the BLP?
  - Just i.i.d. sampling from the **target** population

- Write $Y_i$ in terms of the **projection error**, $Y_i = \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta} + e_i$, and substitute it into $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} &= \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\big(\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta} + e_i\big)\right) \\
  &= \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)\boldsymbol{\beta} + \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i e_i\right) \\
  &= \boldsymbol{\beta} + \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i e_i\right)
  \end{aligned}
  $$

:::

## Consistency of OLS

::: {.incremental}

- By the **law of large numbers**, each sample mean converges to its population mean

  $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime] \qquad \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i e_i \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i e_i] = \mathbf{0}$$

  - Last week we showed that the prediction errors are orthogonal to $X_i$ for the BLP **mechanically**

- The inverse is a **continuous** function, so by the **continuous mapping theorem**

  $$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol{\beta} + \big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}\,\mathbf{0} = \boldsymbol{\beta}$$

- Really, we just need **an LLN** to apply to our sample plug-ins
  - So relaxations of i.i.d that still let us invoke LLN/CLT are fine
  - (e.g. clustered sampling, spatial correlation that dissipates over sufficient distances, etc...)

:::

## Asymptotic normality of OLS

::: {.incremental}

- For the sample mean, the **CLT** gave us $\sqrt{n}(\hat{\mu} - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. The same idea applies to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$
- Multiply the decomposition by $\sqrt{n}$

  $$\sqrt{n}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - \boldsymbol{\beta}\big) = \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)^{-1}}_{\xrightarrow{p}\ \big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}} \ \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i e_i - \mathbf{0}\right)}_{\xrightarrow{d}\ \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\ \boldsymbol{\Omega})}$$

- A **multivariate CLT** applies to the sample mean of the i.i.d. $\mathbf{X}_ie_i$ random vectors and

  $$\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \Var(\mathbf{X}_i e_i) = \mathbb{E}[e_i^2\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]$$

- By **Slutsky's theorem**

::: {.recap-result .fragment}
$\sqrt{n}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - \boldsymbol{\beta}\big) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\Big(\mathbf{0},\ \big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}\,\boldsymbol{\Omega}\,\big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}\Big)$
:::

:::

## The asymptotic variance

::: {.incremental}

- Now let's obtain $\Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$ - the **variance-covariance** matrix of the **sampling distribution** of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$
  - For a $k \times k$ non-random matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and a random vector $\mathbf{Z}$, $\Var(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z}) = \mathbf{A}\,\Var(\mathbf{Z})\,\mathbf{A}^\prime$
    - This is the "matrix" equivalent of "squaring" a constant: $\Var(aZ) = a^2\Var(Z)$
- Applying this to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - \boldsymbol{\beta} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \cdot \sqrt{n}\big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - \boldsymbol{\beta}\big)$

  $$\Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \frac{1}{n}\Var\Bigg(\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)^{-1}}_{\mathbf{A}\ \xrightarrow{p}\ \big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}} \ \underbrace{\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i e_i - \mathbf{0}\right)}_{\mathbf{Z}\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\ \boldsymbol{\Omega})}\Bigg)$$

- The result is a **sandwich**: two slices of **bread** around the **filling**

  $$\underbrace{\Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}_{k \times k} \approx \frac{1}{n} \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}}_{k \times k} \ \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{k \times k} \ \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}}_{k \times k}$$

:::

## The variance-covariance matrix

::: {.incremental}

- Written out, the **variance-covariance matrix** of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is

  $$\Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \begin{pmatrix} \Var(\hat{\beta}_0) & \Cov(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1) & \cdots & \Cov(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_{k-1}) \\ \Cov(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\beta}_0) & \Var(\hat{\beta}_1) & \cdots & \Cov(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\beta}_{k-1}) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \Cov(\hat{\beta}_{k-1}, \hat{\beta}_0) & \Cov(\hat{\beta}_{k-1}, \hat{\beta}_1) & \cdots & \Var(\hat{\beta}_{k-1}) \end{pmatrix}$$

  - The **standard error** of $\hat{\beta}_j$ is the square root of the corresponding **diagonal** entry

:::

## The filling

::: {.incremental}

- $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i e_i] = \mathbf{0}$, so $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is the expectation of an **outer product**

  $$\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \Var(\mathbf{X}_i e_i) = \mathbb{E}\big[(\mathbf{X}_i e_i)(\mathbf{X}_i e_i)^\prime\big] - \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i e_i]\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i e_i]^\prime}_{\mathbf{0}} = \mathbb{E}[e_i^2\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]$$

- Each respondent contributes $\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime$ **weighted** by their squared error

  $$\small \underbrace{\mathbf{X}_i e_i}_{k \times 1} \quad \underbrace{(\mathbf{X}_i e_i)^\prime}_{1 \times k} = e_i^2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ X_{i1} \\ \vdots \\ X_{i,k-1} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_{i1} & \cdots & X_{i,k-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} e_i^2 & e_i^2 X_{i1} & \cdots & e_i^2 X_{i,k-1} \\ e_i^2 X_{i1} & e_i^2 X_{i1}^2 & \cdots & e_i^2 X_{i1} X_{i,k-1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ e_i^2 X_{i,k-1} & e_i^2 X_{i,k-1} X_{i1} & \cdots & e_i^2 X_{i,k-1}^2 \end{pmatrix}$$

:::

## Estimating the variance

::: {.incremental}

- **Plug-in principle** again: replace each expectation with a sample mean and each unobserved $e_i$ with its **residual** $\hat{e}_i = Y_i - \mathbf{X}_i^\prime\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$

  $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X} \qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{e}_i^2\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime$$

- Plug these into the sandwich (the $n$'s cancel)

  $$\begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) &= \frac{1}{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{e}_i^2\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \\
  &= (\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{e}_i^2\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\right)(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}
  \end{aligned}$$

- This is the **heteroskedasticity-consistent** (HC0) or Eicker-Huber-White estimator - usually called **robust** standard errors

:::

## Estimating the variance

::: {.incremental}

- You'll often see the filling written as an equivalent matrix product involving a $n \times n$ matrix $\widehat{\mathbf{D}}$

  $$\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{e}_i^2\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime = \underbrace{\mathbf{X}^\prime}_{k \times n} \ \underbrace{\widehat{\mathbf{D}}}_{n \times n} \ \underbrace{\mathbf{X}}_{n \times k} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}_1 & \mathbf{X}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{X}_n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \hat{e}_1^2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \hat{e}_2^2 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \hat{e}_n^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X}_1^\prime \\ \mathbf{X}_2^\prime \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{X}_n^\prime \end{pmatrix}$$

- Later on, we'll connect this to the **variance-covariance matrix of the errors** in the classical regression setting
  - **Off-diagonals** are $0$: under **i.i.d. sampling**, $e_i$ and $e_j$ are independent
  - **Diagonals** $\sigma_i^2 = \mathbb{E}[e_i^2 \mid \mathbf{X}_i]$ can differ across respondents with different $\mathbf{X}_i$
  - The HC0 estimator plugs in $\hat{e}_i^2$ for each $\sigma_i^2$

:::

## HC0 by hand

- The HC0 variance estimator is a $k \times k$ sandwich

  $$\underbrace{\widehat{\Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}_{k \times k} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}}_{k \times k} \ \underbrace{\mathbf{X}^\prime\widehat{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{X}}_{k \times k} \ \underbrace{(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}}_{k \times k}$$

- Let's take a look at this with a complete regression with both attitude measures **and** the party dummies

```{r}
fit_full <- lm(ft_trump ~ hostile_sexism + racial_resentment + party, data = anes)

X <- model.matrix(fit_full)           # n x k: intercept, two attitudes, two party dummies
dim(X)
e_hat <- resid(fit_full)

bread <- solve(t(X) %*% X)            # (X'X)^{-1}, k x k
D <- diag(e_hat^2)                    # n x n, squared residuals on the diagonal
filling <- t(X) %*% D %*% X           # X'DX, k x k
V_hc0 <- bread %*% filling %*% bread  # k x k

round(sqrt(diag(V_hc0)), 3)           # standard errors: the square roots of the diagonal
```


## HC0 with `sandwich`

- The `sandwich` package computes these for any `lm()` fit

```{r}
library(sandwich)
V_sw <- vcovHC(fit_full, type = "HC0")
round(sqrt(diag(V_sw)), 3)
```

::: {.incremental}

- Careful: the **default** in `vcovHC` is `type = "HC3"` which is a small-sample correction
  - "Robust" standard errors are **consistent** but not **unbiased** - in small samples they tend to be **too small**. 
  - Many corrections proposed in the literature.
  - `HC1` rescales HC0 by $n/(n - k)$ (Stata's `, robust`)
  - `HC2` and `HC3` rescale each $\hat{e}_i^2$ by how much observation $i$ pulls on its own fit

:::

## Confidence intervals and tests

::: {.incremental}

- Asymptotic normality lets us use the same approach to testing as before

  $$\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{\widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_j)} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \qquad \widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_j) = \sqrt{\big[\widehat{\Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big]_{jj}}$$

- 95% **confidence interval**: $\hat{\beta}_j \pm 1.96 \times \widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_j)$
- **Test** of $H_0: \beta_j = 0$: $t = \hat{\beta}_j / \widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_j)$, with two-sided p-value $2\big(1 - \Phi(|t|)\big)$

:::

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
b <- coef(fit_full)
se_hc0 <- sqrt(diag(V_sw))
t_hc0 <- b / se_hc0
cbind(round(cbind(estimate = b, se = se_hc0,
                  lower = b - qnorm(0.975) * se_hc0, upper = b + qnorm(0.975) * se_hc0,
                  t = t_hc0), 3),
      p = signif(2 * pnorm(-abs(t_hc0)), 3))
```

:::

## The sampling distribution of a line

```{r}

# with X) for the sampling distribution animation (samp-anim/samp.js): the

set.seed(812)

sd_t <- c(2, 0.6)
sd_draws <- lapply(seq_len(sd_S), function(s) {

  y <- sd_t[1] + sd_t[2] * x + rnorm(sd_n, 0, 0.2 + 0.2 * x)
  list(x = round(x, 3), y = round(y, 3), b = unname(coef(lm(y ~ x))))
})
sd_data <- jsonlite::toJSON(list(px = lapply(sd_draws[1:sd_K], `[[`, "x"),
                                 py = lapply(sd_draws[1:sd_K], `[[`, "y"),
                                 b0 = round(sapply(sd_draws, function(s) s$b[1]), 4),
                                 b1 = round(sapply(sd_draws, function(s) s$b[2]), 4),
                                 t0 = sd_t[1], t1 = sd_t[2],

                            auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA)
samp_anim <- function(from, to) {

}

## Standard errors for a bivariate regression

::: {.incremental}

- With one regressor, the OLS slope is

  $$\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})\,Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2}$$

- Substitute $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + e_i$. Because $\sum_i (X_i - \bar{X}) = 0$ and $\sum_i (X_i - \bar{X})X_i = \sum_i (X_i - \bar{X})^2$

  $$\hat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})\,e_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2}$$

:::

## Standard errors for a bivariate regression

::: {.incremental}

- Divide the top and the bottom by $n$

  $$\hat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1 = \frac{\overbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})\,e_i}^{\approx\ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu_X)\,e_i}}{\underbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2}_{\xrightarrow{p}\ \Var(X_i)}}$$

- Since $\bar{X} \xrightarrow{p} \mu_X$, the numerator behaves like a sample mean of the i.i.d. $(X_i - \mu_X)e_i$, which have mean $0$ and variance $\mathbb{E}[(X_i - \mu_X)^2 e_i^2]$
- The variance of a sample mean of $n$ i.i.d. terms is $\frac{1}{n}$ times the variance of one term
  - ...and the denominator is (approximately) the constant $\Var(X_i)$, so it comes out squared
- And we get the **sandwich** estimator in scalar form:

  $$\Var(\hat{\beta}_1) \approx \frac{1}{n}\,\frac{\overbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[(X_i - \mu_X)^2 e_i^2\big]}^{\text{filling}}}{\underbrace{\Var(X_i)^2}_{\text{bread}}}$$

:::

## Standard errors for a bivariate regression

::: {.incremental}

- **Plug-in**: replace the expectations with sample means and $e_i$ with $\hat{e}_i$ (the $n$'s cancel)

  $$\begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) &= \frac{1}{n}\,\frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\,\hat{e}_i^2}{\Big(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\Big)^2} \\
  &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\,\hat{e}_i^2}{\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\Big)^2}
  \end{aligned}$$

  and $\widehat{SE}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \sqrt{\widehat{\Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)}$

- Our **standard error** for the slope is **smaller** when we have...
  - ...a larger $n$
  - ...more **spread** in $X_i$
  - ...smaller errors, especially **far** from $\bar{X}$ since each $\hat{e}_i^2$ is weighted by $(X_i - \bar{X})^2$

:::

## Uncertainty about $\hat{Y}$

::: {.incremental}

- Given our standard errors for $\hat{\beta}_0$ and $\hat{\beta}_1$, we may want to know how precise our BLP estimate of $Y$ is at a given $x$

  $$\hat{Y}(x) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x$$

- This is a sum of two random variables, so we need the full **variance-covariance matrix** of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$

  $$\Var\bigg(\hat{Y}(x)\bigg) = \Var(\hat{\beta}_0) + x^2\,\Var(\hat{\beta}_1) + 2x\,\Cov(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1)$$

  - Plug in the HC0 estimates of all three!
- To get the intuition for how the variance changes, re-write the line as: $\hat{Y}(x) = \bar{Y} + \hat{\beta}_1\,(x - \bar{X})$
  - At $\bar{X}$, we have uncertainty about $\bar{Y}$
  - **And** we have uncertainty about how the **slope**, which matters more as we move away from $\bar{X}$
  - So the sampling variance is smallest near $\bar{X}$ and grows as we move away from it, giving a **"bowtie"** shape to the confidence intervals.

:::

## Confidence interval for the regression line

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}

```{r}
# HC0 vcov of the intercept and slope
V <- vcovHC(fit_hs, type = "HC0")
V

grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
se_fit <- sqrt(V[1, 1] + grid^2 * V[2, 2] +
                2 * grid * V[1, 2])

line_ci <- tibble(x = grid,
                  fit = b_hs[1] + b_hs[2] * grid,
                  lower = fit - 1.96 * se_fit,
                  upper = fit + 1.96 * se_fit)
head(line_ci, 3)
```

## Comparing robust SEs with `lm()` defaults

- `coeftest()` from `lmtest` will implement the tests with whatever variance covariance matrix we want to give it

```{r}
#| message: false
library(lmtest)
coeftest(fit_full)                                           # lm() defaults
coeftest(fit_full, vcov = vcovHC(fit_full, type = "HC0"))    # robust (HC0)
```

## Comparing robust SEs with `lm()` defaults

::::

##

::: {.statement style="height: 560px; flex-direction: column;"}
| *T-stat looks too good.*
| *Use robust standard errors—*
| *significance gone.*

[— Keisuke Hirano]{style="font-size: 0.6em; margin-top: 1.2em;"}
:::

## Homoskedasticity

::: {.incremental}

- The **classical** OLS model adds an assumption about the errors: **homoskedasticity**

  $$\mathbb{E}[e_i^2 \mid \mathbf{X}_i] = \sigma^2$$

  - The variance of the errors is **constant** at every value of the covariates

- Under homoskedasticity, the filling simplifies by the **law of iterated expectations**

  $$\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \mathbb{E}[e_i^2\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime] = \mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[e_i^2 \mid \mathbf{X}_i]\,\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime\big] = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]$$

- And the sandwich reduces to...

  $$\Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \approx \frac{1}{n}\big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}\,\sigma^2\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\,\big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\big(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\prime]\big)^{-1}$$

  $$\Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \approx \frac{1}{n}\sigma^2\left(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}$$

:::

## Is homoskedasticity plausible?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center

# The residuals from the full fit by party, jittered, with a bar at +/- one
# residual SD around zero
res_party <- tibble(party = model.frame(fit_full)$party, e = e_hat)
res_sd <- res_party |> summarize(sd = sd(e), n = n(), .by = party)
ggplot(res_party, aes(x = party, y = e, colour = party)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0, alpha = 0.08, size = 2, stroke = 0) +
  geom_errorbar(data = res_sd, aes(x = party, ymin = -sd, ymax = sd), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                width = 0.35, linewidth = 1.4, colour = "#333333") +
  geom_label(data = res_sd, aes(x = party, y = 0, label = sprintf("SD = %.1f", sd)),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, nudge_x = 0.33, size = 6, colour = "#333333",
             fill = "#F7F7F7", label.size = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = party_cols, guide = "none") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual from the full regression") +
  theme_reg
```

::: {.incremental}

- No! The residuals are far more **spread out** for Independents and Republicans than for Democrats
  - What we'd expect for a bounded thermometer: `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(anes$ft_trump[anes$party %in% "Democrat"] == 0))`% of Democrats rate Trump at exactly **0**
  - Can't go any lower!

:::

## Estimating $\sigma^2$

::: {.incremental}

- A natural plug-in for $\sigma^2$ is $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{e}_i^2$. 
  - But like the plug-in sample variance, it is **biased** downward: OLS picks $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ to make the residuals small **in this sample**
- The **unbiased** estimator divides by $n - k$, the number of observations minus the number of coefficients

  $$\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n - k}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{e}_i^2$$

- Related to our earlier results for the unbiased population variance estimator
  - There we divided by $n-1$
  - Here since each estimated coefficient "uses up" one **degree of freedom**, we divide by $n-k$.
- The **classical** OLS variance estimator is therefore

  $$\widehat{\Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \hat{\sigma}^2(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}$$ 


- Default for `summary(lm())`


:::

## Robust or classical?

::: {.incremental}

- **HC** standard errors are consistent whether or not the errors are homoskedastic
  - **Classical** standard errors are only consistent under homoskedasticity

- If homoskedasticity **does** hold, the classical estimator is more precise.
  - But it's rarely a credible assumption!

- In practice: **default** to robust standard errors
  - In 813, we'll talk more about the `HC2` correction (default in `lm_robust()` in the `estimatr` package).
  - "Agnostic" regression

:::

## The classical linear model

::: {.incremental}

- Many textbooks start from a much stronger set of assumptions. Conditional on the $n \times k$ matrix $\mathbf{X}$
  1. **Linearity**: $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{e}$ with $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e} \mid \mathbf{X}] = \mathbf{0}$. The CEF **is** linear
  2. **Full rank**: $\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X}$ is invertible
  3. **Spherical errors**: $\Var(\mathbf{e} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}_n$. Homoskedastic and uncorrelated across observations
  4. (Sometimes) **Normality**: $\mathbf{e} \mid \mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I}_n)$

- The benefit of this is that we get **exact** finite-sample results instead of asymptotic approximations
  - Under 1-3, OLS is **unbiased** and its variance is **exactly** the classical formula

  $$\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}] = \boldsymbol{\beta} \qquad \Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}) = (\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\prime\,\underbrace{\Var(\mathbf{e} \mid \mathbf{X})}_{\sigma^2\mathbf{I}_n}\,\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1} = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}$$

- Our "agnostic" approach so far needed only i.i.d. sampling and the regularity conditions
  - OLS estimates the **BLP**, whatever the CEF looks like, and the robust variance is valid for asymptotic inference on the **BLP**

:::

## SEs and assumptions about the error variances

- With a linear CEF, the "filling" of the sandwich variance can be written in terms of the **variance-covariance matrix of the errors** $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \Var(\mathbf{e} \mid \mathbf{X})$

  $$\Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}) = (\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\,\mathbf{X}^\prime\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{X}\,(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}$$

- Each standard error estimator assumes a different $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$

:::: {.columns .sigma-cols}

::: {.column width="31%"}
**Homoskedastic**

$$\small \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma^2 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma^2 \end{pmatrix}$$

- Constant variance + no cross-unit covariance
- Plug in $\hat{\sigma}^2$: **classical**
:::

::: {.column width="31%" .fragment}
**Heteroskedastic**

$$\small \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_2^2 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma_n^2 \end{pmatrix}$$

- Non-constant variance + no cross-unit covariance
- Plug in $\hat{e}_i^2$: **HC**
:::

::: {.column width="38%" .fragment}
**Clustered**

$$\small \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc|c} \sigma_1^2 & \sigma_{12} & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \cdots \\ \sigma_{12} & \sigma_2^2 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & & \\ \hline 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma_j^2 & \sigma_{jk} & \cdots & \cdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma_{jk} & \sigma_k^2 & \cdots & \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \\ \hline \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & & \ddots \end{array}\right)$$

- **Arbitrary** correlation within clusters but none **across**
- Plug in $\hat{e}_i\hat{e}_j$ within clusters: **cluster-robust**
:::

::::

## The Gauss-Markov theorem

::: {.incremental}

- Under assumptions 1-3, OLS is the **B**est **L**inear **U**nbiased **E**stimator (**BLUE**)
  - **Linear**: $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{Y}$ for some $k \times n$ matrix $\mathbf{C}$ that depends only on $\mathbf{X}$. OLS has $\mathbf{C} = (\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\prime$
  - **Unbiased**: $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}] = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} = \boldsymbol{\beta}$ for every $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, which requires $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}_k$
  - **Best**: no other linear unbiased estimator has a smaller variance for any coefficient (or linear combination of coefficients)

- **Proof sketch**: write an alternative estimator that deviates from OLS: $\mathbf{C} = (\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\prime + \mathbf{D}$. 
  - Unbiasedness requires $\mathbf{D}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$, so the cross terms drop out

  $$\small \Var(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}) = \sigma^2\mathbf{C}\mathbf{C}^\prime = \sigma^2\big[(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{D}^\prime}_{\mathbf{0}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{D}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\prime\mathbf{X})^{-1}}_{\mathbf{0}} + \mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\prime\big] = \Var(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \mid \mathbf{X}) + \sigma^2\mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\prime$$

  - The $j$th diagonal entry of $\mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\prime$ is a sum of squares, $\sum_i D_{ji}^2 \geq 0$, so every coefficient's variance can only go **up**

:::

## What BLUE does and doesn't buy us

::: {.incremental}

- "Best" only among estimators that are **linear** in $\mathbf{Y}$ **and** **unbiased**
  - A **biased** estimator can have a lower mean squared error (e.g. a penalized regression)

- It depends on **homoskedasticity**:
  - **Weighted** least squares, which down-weights the noisier observations, can do better if we know the form of the heteroskedasticity
  - And the classical standard errors are **wrong**

- It needs a **linear CEF** for unbiasedness
  - Without it, OLS is still consistent for the **BLP**, but the finite-sample results no longer hold

:::

## Hierarchy of assumptions

<!-- Each column is something we want from OLS; each row an assumption; a
     check means that goal needs that assumption. Reading left to right, every
     column needs everything the one before it did, plus one more row. -->

<div class="assume-table"><table>
<thead><tr>
  <th></th>
  <th>Compute<br>\(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\)</th>
  <th>Consistent<br>for the BLP</th>

  <th>Unbiased<br>for the CEF</th>

</tr></thead>

  <tr class="sep"><td>i.i.d. sampling + regularity conditions</td><td></td><td class="y">✓</td><td class="y">✓</td><td class="y">✓</td><td class="y">✓</td><td class="y">✓</td></tr>
  <tr class="sep"><td>Linear CEF, \(\mathbb{E}[e_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i] = 0\)</td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td class="y">✓</td><td class="y">✓</td><td class="y">✓</td></tr>
  <tr class="sep"><td>Homoskedasticity, \(\Var(e_i \mid \mathbf{X}_i) = \sigma^2\)</td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td class="y">✓</td><td class="y">✓</td></tr>
  <tr class="sep"><td>Normal errors</td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td class="y">✓</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
```

::: {.incremental}

- **Very little** gets us the BLP and valid (asymptotic) inference on it: i.i.d. sampling, robust standard errors and a CLT
- Saying anything about the **CEF** itself requires it to be linear (in whatever $\mathbf{X}$ we provide).
- Homoskedasticity and normality get **efficiency** and **exact** small-sample inference, but they're rarely credible

:::
